               COMMENTS OF EVERSOURCE ENERGY SERVICE COMPANY

           Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules and Regulations, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211,

Eversource Energy Service Company ("Eversource"), on behalf of its public utility affiliates,1

respectfully submits these comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

("Commission" or "FERC") regarding the application of NextEra Energy, Inc. ("NextEra") and

Dominion Energy, Inc. ("Dominion," and with NextEra, the “Joint Applicants”) pursuant to

sections 203(a)(1) and 203(a)(2) of the Federal Power Act2 (“FPA”) for FERC authorization of a

merger of the two entities (the "Transaction"). Eversource’s comments focus on the proposed

Transaction’s potential anti-competitive effects and expected adverse effects on energy rates in

New England’s wholesale electricity markets, including bilateral clean energy markets, and

recommends conditions of approval to protect consumers from these adverse effects.

      I.      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

           Eversource does not oppose the Transaction but, as set forth herein, proposes specific

conditions to mitigate market power risk associated with the Transaction that are not consistent

with the public interest. Through the Transaction, Dominion will merge into NextEra.3 The

This means Merged NextEra will: (1) control all of the nuclear power produced in New England,

which accounts for about one-fourth of the region’s annual energy supply and more than two-thirds

of New England’s zero carbon emitting energy (or “clean energy”) in New England each year; and

(2) have market power over on-site nuclear power data center development in New England, which

        Based on these market power concerns, Eversource urges the Commission to approve the

Transaction subject to an appropriate combination of the following conditions, explained in more

            1. Divest one of the nuclear plants to a third party.

            2. Require a long-term power purchase agreement at market-based rates for at least

                one of the nuclear plants.

            3. Restrict post-merger affiliates from collusion and collaboration in market decisions.

            4. Implement independent offer protocols.

            5. Independently review clean energy offers.

            6. Require periodic compliance audits.

            7. Assess penalties for the exercise of market power in clean energy markets.

            8. Review the impact of onsite data centers on electricity prices.

            9. Require establishment of a large load tariff.

            10. Divest NextEra’s Seabrook transmission substation.

 Because the Transaction has the potential to affect energy production, capacity availability, and

wholesale market prices in the New England region for many years, it is important to carefully

consider whether the Transaction is in the public interest. The Transaction is expected to have

anti-competitive effects and cause increased consumer energy rates in New England and its

interconnected markets.

      II.      BACKGROUND

            A. Description of Eversource

            Eversource’s parent company, Eversource Energy, is a public utility holding company

under the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 20054 that owns and operates over 4,000 miles

of transmission facilities in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New Hampshire, has electric

distribution facilities in each of those states, and serves approximately 4.4 million electric and

natural gas customers in New England.

            Eversource Energy is committed to ensuring reliable and clean energy at competitive prices

for its customers and, as a load-serving entity and owner of critical electric infrastructure within

New England, has a direct and substantial interest in preserving competitive wholesale electricity

markets, maintaining adequate safeguards against the exercise of market power, and promoting

the development of clean energy resources. Eversource submits these comments to assist the

Commission's review of the Transaction and to ensure that any approval is consistent with the

public interest, pursuant to FPA § 203, 16 U.S.C. § 824b.

            B. Overview of the Proposed Merger

            As proposed, the Transaction would create the largest power producer in the United States,

with an enterprise value near the highest levels for an energy firm, close to the enterprise value of

      III.      PUBLIC INTEREST CONSIDERATIONS

            A. FPA Section 203 Standard of Review

            Under the Federal Power Act, the Commission must determine that a proposed transaction

is consistent with the public interest.9 To determine if a transaction is consistent with the public

interest, the Commission considers three factors: (1) the effect on competition; (2) the effect on

rates; and (3) the effect on regulation.10 The Commission adopted the five-step framework set out

in the Antitrust Agencies’ 1992 Horizontal Merger Guidelines (1992 Guidelines) as the basic

framework for evaluating the competitive effects of proposed mergers.11 The Commission also

adopted an analytic screen (Competitive Analysis Screen), based on the 1992 Guidelines and

outlined in Appendix A of the Merger Policy Statement, which focuses on whether the merger

would significantly increase concentration of ownership and control in relevant markets.12 The

Commission analyzes market concentration using the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)

thresholds, a widely accepted measure of market concentration.13 The HHI is calculated by

squaring the market share of each firm competing in the market and summing the results.14 The

HHI increases as (i) the number of firms in the market decreases; and/or (ii) as the disparity in size

between those firms increases.15

            Where a proposed transaction results in significant screen failures and adverse effects on

competition, the Commission has conditionally authorized the transaction. For example, in 2022,

the Commission conditionally authorized the Duke Energy and Progress Energy merger

    IV.      Eversource's Competitive Concerns and the Need for Appropriate Mitigation
            Measures

         A. Eversource Does Not Oppose the Merger Subject to Appropriate Conditions

         Because Merged NextEra would control a larger portfolio of generation and clean energy

assets, the Transaction could create or enhance market power in portions of the ISO-NE region,

particularly as New England's energy markets become increasingly dependent upon clean energy

resources and associated environmental products.

         Accordingly, Eversource respectfully submits that any Commission approval should be

conditioned on the measures proposed herein to prevent the exercise of market power and to

preserve competitive opportunities for market participants and consumers.

         B. Potential Effects on Clean Energy and Competition

         Combined, nearly 25 percent of the energy that ISO-NE procures through its centralized

energy markets are produced by the generation assets owned by the Joint Applicants. Bodell Aff.,

¶ 29. Joint Applicants produce approximately two-thirds of the clean energy produced and sold

through ISO-NE competitive energy markets throughout the year. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 29-32, Fig. 9,

Fig. 10. HHI indicators confirm that the Merged Entity will have an excessive concentration of

clean energy capacity and associated clean energy supplies. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 32-34. Ultimately,

expert Tanya Bodell anticipates the Transaction “grants a single entity control over more than 75

percent of New England’s zero carbon emitting generation supplies (or “clean energy”) and more

than 40 percent of New England’s qualified clean energy capacity.” Bodell Aff., ¶ 5.

         The New England region is experiencing a fundamental transformation in its electric

supply portfolio.     State clean energy policies, decarbonization requirements, renewable

procurement programs, and resource retirements are increasing the importance of renewable

generation, energy storage resources, and related clean energy products.

                                                9
        As ownership of these resources becomes more concentrated, the potential for market

participants to influence prices, procurement outcomes, or competitive opportunities

correspondingly increase. As calculated by industry expert Tanya Bodell, the Merged NextEra,

under conservative assumptions, exceeds FERC’s Merger Guidelines for ISO-NE supplies, clean

energy qualified capacity, and clean energy supplies. Bodell Aff., ¶ 34.

       Even absent deliberate market manipulation, increased concentration by the Transaction

may reduce competitive pressure, encourage physical and economic withholding, discourage entry

by smaller developers, and contribute to higher prices for energy, capacity, Regional Greenhouse

Gas Initiative (“RGGI”) carbon credits, GIS certificates for carbon free generation, and clean

energy contracts. Those increased costs ultimately flow through to retail consumers in New

England, including Eversource's customers. For example, NextEra and Dominion previously

competed against each other for clean energy Requests for Proposals (“RFPs”) and were the

primary competitors in a 2018 Connecticut clean energy RFP. Bodell Aff., ¶ 85. By combining

entities that were formerly competitors that negotiated against each other into one entity that owns

both of New England’s nuclear power plants, the Merged Entity will have increased negotiating

power for future clean energy RFPs, there will be less competition for bilateral power purchase

agreements, and it is likely that energy costs will increase for both ISO-NE wholesale market

participants and regulated retail customers. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 80-82.

       Because the Transaction results in Merged NextEra owning disproportionate market power,

effectively dominating New England’s clean energy generation, this consequently decreases

competition. Pursuant to the FPA section 203 analysis, where the first factor is the “effect on

market concentration” and therefore competition, the Transaction is not in the public interest.




                                                10
         Eversource is particularly concerned that enhanced market power within clean energy

markets could lead to higher long-term costs for carbon-free generation and associated

environmental attributes. Because several states in New England have decarbonization policies

and clean energy procurement programs, large purchasers of clean energy increasingly rely upon

competitive solicitations and market-based procurement processes. Preserving robust competition

among clean energy suppliers is essential to ensuring that customers receive the benefits of New

England’s clean energy transition at the lowest reasonable cost. The second FPA section 203 factor

is the “effect on rates.” This Transaction may increase energy costs for New England consumers

through higher ISO-NE energy market prices, more costly clean energy procurements, and higher

RGGI carbon credit prices, further demonstrating that this merger is not in New England’s public

interest.

        C. Potential Effect on Data Centers and Energy Supplies for Wholesale and Retail
           Customers

        In addition to increasing the concentration of asset ownership in clean energy, the proposed

merger would increase the incentive for Joint Applicants to consolidate market concentration even

further through participating in, influencing, and directly controlling onsite data center

development behind-the-meter at their generation facilities in New England. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 55-

62, 135. Due to a growing trend of co-locating data centers with onsite existing generation

facilities, including nuclear power plants, and Joint Applicants’ prior and announced efforts to do

so at Millstone and Seabrook, the Transaction creates even stronger incentives for Merged NextEra

to develop data centers at Millstone and/or Seabrook. In 2024, Dominion Energy tried developing

a data center in Waterford, Connecticut at the Millstone Power Station, where a nuclear plant

 provides more than 90% of Connecticut’s carbon-free power and generates enough electricity for

almost 2 million homes annually.19 Bodell Aff., ¶ 56.

        However, local residents successfully opposed the data center and cited monopoly

concerns.20 In January 2024, the Connecticut Siting Council denied the data center petition.

Bodell Aff., ¶ 58. New Hampshire has been encouraging the development of data centers, and

NextEra has announced its intention to develop onsite data centers at Seabrook, potentially with

its own generation. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 60-61. By owning the Seabrook and Millstone nuclear power

plants, the Merged Entity has the ability to enter contracts to host onsite data centers at these

locations and sell capacity and energy directly to those large load customers. The proposed merger

would incentivize the Joint Applicants to withdraw capacity and energy from the market, directly

and through onsite data center offtake agreements (as is currently being explored by both Millstone

and Seabrook). This supply reduction would drive up wholesale electricity prices, state RFP

procurement prices, and translate into higher costs for ratepayers. Bodell Aff., ¶ 55.

        Thus, the Transaction could result in Merged NextEra trying to physically withdraw

nuclear capacity and energy through direct sales to onsite large load customers, to the benefit of

its broader portfolio and the detriment of New England’s wholesale and retail electricity customers.

More concretely, a data center at Millstone means that some of the nuclear capacity and energy

that ordinarily went towards supplying New England households, would instead be diverted

towards powering the onsite data center. This reduces the supply available to serve residential

       D. Potential Effects on Electricity Costs

       Because the Transaction is anticipated to result in higher market concentration, another

natural consequence is increased energy prices. Bodell Aff., ¶ 36. According to Ms. Bodell, the

currently high concentration of each nuclear power plant is close to a duopoly. Id. Combined, the

clean energy assets of each of the Joint Applicants will create something closer to a monopoly. Id.

This implies that both ISO-NE energy prices and state-led clean energy procurements’ prices will

increase post-merger if the existing New England assets of Joint Applicants are combined. Id. Ms.

Bodell’s calculations predict that “prices could rise by 23 percent or $8.83/MWh over the course

of the year in the most extreme scenario.” Bodell Aff., ¶ 68. Specifically, the impact of on-site

data centers is that the data center will consumer energy that ordinarily would provide power to

residential or commercial consumers. As the amount of nuclear capacity dedicated to onsite data

centers increases, the cost to ISO-NE wholesale energy market customers also increases by a range

of $177 million at 300 MW to $983 million at 1,500 MW annually under 2024 market conditions,

representing a 4 percent and 21 percent cost increase respectively. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 71-72, Fig. 15.

Additionally, the proposed Transaction will negatively impact the clean energy prices under pre-

merger versus post-merger RFPs. Average clean energy PPA prices increase by more than 50

percent under the most favorable conditions examined. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 45-46, Fig. 11.

       As stated previously, under FPA Section 203, the Commission considers the effect that a

proposed transaction will have on rates, whether that effect is adverse, and whether any adverse

 effect will be mitigated or offset by benefits that are likely to result from the proposed transaction.23

However, Joint Applicants do not even attempt to quantify the potential benefits to New England

customers if the proposed merger were to proceed. See, e.g., NextEra and Dominion Joint

Application for Authorization Under Section 203 of the Federal Power Act, July 15, 2026, Docket

No. EC26-131-000.

     V.      Conditions Are Necessary to Protect Competition and Consumers

          To address these concerns, Eversource respectfully submits that the Commission should

consider imposing merger conditions designed to avoid, mitigate, or limit increased market power

resulting from the Transaction. Bodell Aff., ¶¶ 138-139. Such conditions could include:

             1. Divestiture of Nuclear Units: Require the divestiture of either Seabrook or

                 Millstone nuclear power plant to an entity other than Merged NextEra or its

                 affiliates. If both nuclear power plants are to be sold, ensure that ownership and

                 control of each nuclear facility in New England remain separate.

             2. Long-Term PPA: Require Merged NextEra to enter into a long-term contract for

                 the output of at least one of the nuclear units (i.e., a Purchased Power Agreement

                 or PPA) at market-based rates prior to consummation of the merger in order to

                 mitigate market power concerns in New England’s clean energy markets.

             3. Affiliate Restrictions: Place explicit restrictions on interactions and preferential

                 treatment of affiliated companies, generation companies, transmission companies,

                 and developers of the Merged Entity so as to prevent cross-sector exercise of market

       This appendix provides support for the game theory model used to calculate the impact of
the proposed merger on clean energy solicitation (i.e., RFP) outcomes under various assumptions.


C.1    Game Theory Methodology
       Game theory is a field of economics that studies strategic behavior. It is used in situations
where an economic actor’s best decision depends on its’ own objectives and the decisions of other
economic actors. Game theory models consist of three core elements:
       1. Players – The set of economic actors whose decisions collectively determine the
           outcome of interest.
       2. Actions – The complete set of decisions available to each player.
       3. Payoffs – A measurement of the value received by each player for a given outcome.
           For every possible combination of actions, there must exist one payoff per player.

       Once all three elements are defined, the game can be solved by finding its Nash Equilibria.
There are two types of Nash Equilibria:
       •   Pure Strategy Nash Equilibria – A combination of actions, one per player, such that
           no player has a unilateral incentive to change their chosen action. A game can have
           zero, one, or multiple such equilibria.
       •   Mixed Strategy Nash Equilibria – A combination of strategies such that no player
           has a unilateral incentive to change their chosen strategy, where a strategy is defined
           as a probability distribution over each player’s action set. A game can have one or
           multiple such equilibria.

These concepts can be illustrated through a simple game theory construct. We assume there are two
“players” in the electricity supply game: Millstone and Seabrook. They compete to satisfy a fixed
market demand of 100 MWh of electricity. Each plant can select an offer price from two discrete
options: $48/MWh or $50/MWh, and will not sell below $40/MWh which is the reservation price.

C.3    Technical Approach
       The games are solved using an iterative best-response method. This approach works by
randomly choosing one starting action for each player. Next, players take turns updating their
chosen action so as to best respond to the actions of all other players. If an entire round passes
without any player choosing to change their action, a pure strategy Nash Equilibrium has been
reached and the model stops.

C.3.1 Objective Function

C.3.2 Solution
       Some games do not have any pure strategy Nash Equilibria. In these cases, the iterative best
response approach will result in an endless loop of action choices. When the model detects such a
loop, it stops the iterative best approach process. The set of player actions that appeared in the loop
are used to construct a subgame, which is solved for a mixed strategy Nash Equilibria.
       The iterative best response method only finds one of potentially multiple Nash Equilibria.
The program therefore runs each game ten times in both its pre-merger and post-merger forms, each
time using different randomizing seeds that randomize the starting actions and player orders. The
reported results are the average outcomes across all ten runs.

C.5    Reinforcement Learning to Test Uncertainty
       The analysis also evaluated the sensitivity of outcomes by introducing uncertainty by
allowing firms to learn about the procurement environment through repeated simulated interactions
rather than being given the optimal bidding strategy directly. In each simulation, firms choose bids,
observe whether and how much of their offered capacity is accepted, and receive the resulting
profits as rewards.

placing greater with on strategies that have performed well while continuing to explore alternative
bids. This process is repeated over many simulated events until bidding behavior stabilized. Unlike
the game theory model that solves for equilibrium strategies given market conditions, this approach
generates offer behavior through an adaptative learning process. Ultimately, this allows the model
to capture uncertainty about competitors’ and buyer behavior.
